title: Mixology Certification

jokes.text: The group sings only the last two words of Happy Birthday — 'To you!' — because Troy is a Jehovah's Witness
jokes.setup: We hear only the last two words of Happy Birthday being sung, which is strange and abrupt
jokes.punchline: Jeff explains Troy is a Jehovah's Witness who doesn't celebrate birthdays, so the group stripped the song to its bare minimum to stay compliant
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold open structure: the strangeness is established before we understand it, and the explanation is both logical and absurd. The image of a group singing only two words is inherently funny, and grounding it in a real religious practice adds earned specificity. Strong character integration because only this show would think to dramatize this detail about Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Study Group
dialogue.line: Happy birthday to you, happy birthday to you, happy birthday dear [person], happy birthday to you.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, why do we only sing it to them? What about the rest of us? Are we not happy for their birthday?

jokes.text: "Hello during a random dessert, the month and day of which coincide numerically with your expulsion from a uterus."
jokes.setup: Annie and Jeff tried to make the birthday cake language Jehovah's Witness-compliant
jokes.punchline: The resulting cake inscription is a hyper-clinical, bureaucratic re-description of a birthday in the most antiseptic language possible, ending on 'expulsion from a uterus'
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke of the cold open and one of the episode's best. The escalating clinical language is brilliantly constructed — 'month and day of which coincide numerically' already gets you, but 'expulsion from a uterus' is a perfect landing. It rewards the audience's intelligence, is instantly quotable, and the commitment to the bit (actually putting this on a cake) is fully earned. Comparable in craft to the 8.0 anchor — slightly above it for the originality of concept and the specificity of the phrasing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We can't sing 'Happy Birthday' because Shirley's a Jehovah's Witness. So we need to come up with something else.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We acknowledge the passage of time and your continued presence among us.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's perfect.

jokes.text: "Happy expulsion, Troy."
jokes.setup: Jeff just read the verbose cake inscription aloud
jokes.punchline: Jeff immediately reduces the entire clinical inscription to a casual two-word callback, delivered deadpan
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. The joke is entirely in the compression — taking an absurdly long inscription and collapsing it to 'Happy expulsion.' It works as a callback to joke #2, and it's exactly the kind of casual wit that defines Jeff Winger as a character. Very high quotability. The structure is near-perfect: big windup, tiny punch.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Guys, we really need to study for this exam. Why does everyone keep finding excuses to avoid the library?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie, come on. Britta just found out her coffee has exactly the right foam-to-liquid ratio. We have to celebrate that.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not a real reason to skip studying!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Actually, foam ratios are very serious business.

jokes.text: "Last week we had fondue and played Boggle because Shirley's niece took her first bath. With bubbles."
jokes.setup: Jeff is complaining that the group uses any excuse to avoid studying
jokes.punchline: The example he uses — a niece's first bubble bath as a party-worthy milestone — is so minor it perfectly illustrates the problem, and Shirley's sincere interjection 'With bubbles. Thank you, it's a milestone.' makes it land harder
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: Jeff's example is already funny, but Shirley defending the bubble bath as a genuine milestone is what seals it. Good character integration — Shirley's earnest defensiveness is very on-brand. The 'With bubbles' emphasis is a small but precise comedic addition.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Don't you judge me! My niece took her first bath today, and that is a milestone!

jokes.text: Pierce says nobody noticed his birthday last week. The group gasps and then immediately fabricates an elaborate birthday party he supposedly had, insisting he doesn't remember because of his painkillers.
jokes.setup: Pierce bitterly complains that his birthday was last week and nobody cared
jokes.punchline: The group immediately invents a lavish party on the spot and blames Pierce's painkiller-impaired memory when he questions it — the lie escalating in real time ('This is the best party of my life!' '...Nutritious.')
jokes.explanation: The joke has two good layers: the group's callousness toward Pierce (which is consistent characterization) and the increasing absurdity of the cover story. The '...Nutritious.' non-sequitur is the funniest single beat — Pierce apparently said something nutritious-related at this fake party, which is a perfectly weird detail. Good group dynamics comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Nobody remembered my birthday. I can't believe you all forgot.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, we threw you a surprise party last night.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You did?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, it was at Señor Chang's. You were there.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, I don't remember any of it.

jokes.text: "Yeah, you still owe me for the keg deposit." Pierce: "Oh, you think I don't know that?"
jokes.setup: Jeff is continuing to fabricate details of the fake birthday party
jokes.punchline: Jeff casually invents a keg deposit detail, and Pierce — now fully committed to believing the party happened — defensively confirms he knows he owes the money, playing along with a fiction
jokes.explanation: A good button to the fake-party sequence. Pierce's indignant 'Oh, you think I don't know that?' is funny because he's angry about a debt he doesn't actually owe for a party that didn't happen. His wounded pride at the suggestion he might be forgetful is well-observed character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Nutritious!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, Pierce, that's not—

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I was testing you guys.

jokes.text: "Kickpuncher: Detroit?! No way! This is sold out everywhere!" Jeff: "Not everywhere. I got a cousin in Detroit. They're not crazy about it up there."
jokes.setup: Troy is thrilled about his birthday present — a sold-out movie called Kickpuncher: Detroit
jokes.punchline: Jeff reveals he got it from a cousin in Detroit because Detroit apparently has no enthusiasm for a movie named after their city
jokes.explanation: Clean setup/punchline with a good implicit joke about Detroit's reputation. The name 'Kickpuncher: Detroit' is itself funny — it's the kind of dumb action movie sequel that adds a city name. Jeff's explanation is delivered with perfect casualness.

jokes.text: "I broke my legs, not my gender."
jokes.setup: Someone (likely Jeff or Troy) moves to help Pierce open/handle something, presumably because he's in a wheelchair with broken legs
jokes.punchline: Pierce snaps that his injury doesn't change his masculine self-sufficiency — framing gendered behavior as a physical condition
jokes.explanation: Five words that reveal a character. 'I broke my legs, not my gender' is both funny and illuminating — it's Pierce's toxic masculinity rendered in maximum economy. The logic is internally consistent in a ridiculous way (gender as a physical faculty). Very quotable. Strong character integration because only Pierce thinks this way and would say it this bluntly.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I can't believe Kickpuncher: Detroit is sold out everywhere!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, Detroit residents aren't too happy about how the city's being portrayed in the movie.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What do you mean? It's Kickpuncher!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Exactly. They're tired of being the punchline.

jokes.text: Abed rattles off birthday trivia: Tyra Banks (groans), Marissa Tomei (approval), Claude Renoir (enthusiastic 'Yes!'), then segues to Chinese zodiac and Pierce claiming to be a horse like Troy
jokes.setup: Abed announces he has birthday facts to share while everyone else is doing something else
jokes.punchline: The group's reactions calibrate exactly which celebrities are cool (Marissa Tomei) vs. uncool (Tyra Banks), and Abed delivers all of it with complete neutrality. The 'Jackpot' for Claude Renoir is a perfect nerd in-joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed bit — unprompted data dump delivered without affect. The joke is in the contrast between his flatness and the group's opinionated reactions. 'Jackpot' for a French cinematographer is a great Community-specific nerd joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I don't need your help. I can handle my own cake. Why does everyone always assume I need assistance? I'm perfectly capable of managing dessert on my own. Stop trying to control me.

jokes.text: "No, I'm pretty sure I'm a snake. I remember, because I'm determined, self-possessed and mendacious."
jokes.setup: Pierce claims to be a horse on the Chinese zodiac like Troy; Britta corrects that she's the horse
jokes.punchline: Pierce recalls being a snake and proudly lists 'mendacious' (meaning deceptive/lying) among the positive traits he identifies with — entirely unaware it's a negative quality
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character jokes. Pierce proudly claiming 'mendacious' as a positive self-descriptor — not knowing or not caring what it means — is perfect. It works on multiple levels: his obliviousness, his genuine belief in his own positive qualities, and the irony that he's inadvertently accurate. The parallel structure ('self-possessed' appears in both Britta's horse description and Pierce's snake description, then 'mendacious' replaces 'gregarious') is elegant writing. Strong case for 8+ — this is exactly the kind of joke that only works with this specific character.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Troy was born on this day in 1989, the same year as the fall of the Berlin Wall, the Exxon Valdez disaster, and the release of Batman. Also, it's the birthday of triplets who went on to become moderately successful character actors in the 1970s, one of whom was the stand-in for a stunt double on a Schwarzenegger film, and that stunt double's gaffer had a son who was a key grip on a direct-to-video action movie in 1994.

jokes.text: Pierce reveals Troy is actually turning 21, not 20, because "everyone is 10 for two years, because fifth grade is really hard for everyone."
jokes.setup: Pierce is confused about the Chinese zodiac math and reveals Troy was born in 1989, not 1990, making him older than he thought
jokes.punchline: Pierce's explanation for why everyone is 10 for two years — because fifth grade is hard — is delivered as universal folk wisdom, as if this is a commonly accepted fact
jokes.explanation: Pierce's false wisdom delivered with total confidence is a reliable but well-executed bit. 'Everyone is 10 for two years because fifth grade is really hard for everyone' has the quality of a real folk belief that someone might have actually convinced themselves of. The specificity of fifth grade (not fourth, not middle school) makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, if I failed math, does that mean I have to repeat the grade? Because if everyone had to repeat grades when they failed, nobody would ever graduate. We'd all just be in high school forever. Actually, that's not a bad point. Think about it: every single person who ever failed a class would have to repeat it. That's like, half the population still in third grade.

jokes.text: "Mom, how many lies have I been living?!"
jokes.setup: Troy has just learned he's actually 21, not 20, and is processing this revelation
jokes.punchline: Troy's reaction escalates from surprise to existential crisis, addressing an absent mother with melodramatic weight — treating the minor age miscalculation as a fundamental deception
jokes.explanation: Troy's gift for operatic emotional responses to mundane situations is well-deployed here. Calling out to mom about 'how many lies have I been living' over a one-year age discrepancy (caused by Pierce's nonsense math) is perfectly pitched. The plural 'lies' implies a whole edifice of deception built on this one error.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, if I was born in 1989 and it's 2010, that means I'm only 21, not 22?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: My whole life is a lie! I've been living as the wrong age! Do you know what this means?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I need to redo my entire childhood! I'm going back to get my learner's permit!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Everyone at Greendale thinks I'm a fraud! I'm basically a teenager impostor!

jokes.text: "This party just became unacceptable. We're going out." / "Too many lame ones. This is real." / "Well, Shirley, think of it as Troy taking his first bath, only the bubbles are his manhood."
jokes.setup: Jeff convinces everyone they should go to a bar for Troy's 21st; Shirley pushes back citing their earlier complaints about too many parties
jokes.punchline: Jeff callbacks the bubble bath joke from earlier and reframes Troy's 21st birthday as a masculine milestone using the same framework Shirley used to justify the niece's bath
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed callback that uses Shirley's own logic against her. 'The bubbles are his manhood' is an absurd but internally consistent extension of the bath metaphor. Gets a rewatch bonus because on second viewing you appreciate how precisely it mirrors the earlier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know, bathing a baby is like becoming a man. You start out all excited, you get in there, realize you have no idea what you're doing, and by the end you're just hoping nobody notices you've made a terrible mess.

jokes.text: "Yes. I wanna bathe in manhood."
jokes.setup: Jeff uses the bath metaphor to describe Troy's 21st as a masculine coming-of-age
jokes.punchline: Troy enthusiastically agrees with the metaphor without realizing how it sounds, earnestly expressing desire to 'bathe in manhood'
jokes.explanation: Troy's earnest embrace of the unintentionally homoerotic phrase is a classic character beat. His complete lack of ironic awareness is what makes it work — he's genuinely excited. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is, I need to bathe in the tears of my enemies?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, Troy, that's not—

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Because I can do that. I will do that. I'm gonna start right now.

jokes.text: "No, but I also haven't been to Beirut. But I'm sure I will go one day, because... because I hear they have lots of important cultural..." [interrupted]
jokes.setup: Jeff challenges Britta for dismissing L Street without having been there
jokes.punchline: Britta tries to use Beirut (a war-torn city) as a parallel example of somewhere she hasn't been but would go, then realizes mid-sentence the analogy is falling apart and trails off incoherently
jokes.explanation: Classic Britta self-undermining: she starts an argument she can't finish, comparing a bar to Beirut to seem worldly and open-minded, then can't complete the thought. The trailing off is the joke. Good character integration — this is very specifically Britta's brand of performative progressivism that collapses under scrutiny.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: L Street? More like L-lame Street.

jokes.text: "What makes it real?" Jeff: "Well, Shirley, think of it as Troy taking his first bath..." Shirley: "Those are milkshakes, Shirley." Pierce's suggestion of Peg Leg Pablo's serving 'virgin mudslides'
jokes.setup: Pierce suggests Peg Leg Pablo's as a compromise bar, citing their virgin mudslides as a selling point
jokes.punchline: Jeff flatly corrects that virgin mudslides are just milkshakes — deflating Pierce's enthusiasm and implicitly pointing out the silliness of a bar that serves milkshakes
jokes.explanation: Functional observational humor — a virgin mudslide is literally a milkshake. The deflation is clean but not especially original. Gets the job done.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Have you been to L Street?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh, it's like... it's like if Narnia and a boutique had a baby, and that baby was raised by someone with really good taste and a decent budget, and then that baby grew up and opened a store where you could buy the most beautiful things, and every time you went there it was like Christmas morning, but also like you were discovering a secret that only the coolest people knew about, and...

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I?

jokes.text: "Fine. I'll get Annie an ID." Annie: "A fake ID??" Jeff: "It will be real. It just won't be yours."
jokes.setup: Jeff offers to solve Annie's age problem
jokes.punchline: His semantic distinction — 'It will be real, it just won't be yours' — is a perfectly lawyer-brained rationalization that reframes identity fraud as a technicality
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Jeff's legal-loophole brain produces a perfectly constructed semantic distinction that is both funny and completely in character. 'It will be real, it just won't be yours' has the rhythm and structure of a great one-liner — the pause before 'it just won't be yours' is where the laugh lives. Very quotable, very Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're being so hipster right now.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm not a hipster. I was into obscure things way before they were cool.

jokes.text: "Count of three: name the least offensive bar you've ever been to. One, two, three." Both Jeff and Britta say "Flannahan's Hole" simultaneously.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta have been unable to agree on a bar; Jeff proposes a simultaneous blurt to cut the debate
jokes.punchline: They both name the same bar — 'Flannahan's Hole' — instantly, revealing they've been arguing about bars they both actually like, while also delivering the inherently funny name 'Flannahan's Hole' as a simultaneous punchline
jokes.explanation: Double payoff: the structural reveal (they like the same bar) and the name itself ('Hole' is crude but the 'Flannahan's' makes it feel genuinely Irish-dive-bar). The simultaneous delivery is key — it shows their shared sensibility beneath the posturing. Gets a rewatch bonus because it foreshadows the final reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: We should go to Peg Leg Pablo's for virgin mudslides.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: A virgin mudslide is just chocolate milk.

jokes.text: "I'm not a disabled! I don't need people helping me do normal things and doting over me... Why don't you just leave...? Okay, I'll beat you there!"
jokes.setup: Someone offers Pierce a ride given his broken legs and wheelchair
jokes.punchline: Pierce's indignant refusal of help — asserting independence — immediately collapses into a competitive declaration that he'll beat them to the bar despite being in a wheelchair
jokes.explanation: Pierce's broken-leg subplot is mined well here. 'I'm not a disabled' is a grammatically wrong version of a correct statement, which is funny. The pivot from 'I don't need help' to 'I'll beat you there' is a good escalating reversal — the competitive drive undermines the independence claim immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, you have a fake ID?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, I have a real ID. It's just not mine.

jokes.text: Annie looks at the fake ID: "I don't think this girl looks very much like me." Jeff: "Come on. She's a white brunette." Annie: "So is Anne Hathaway."
jokes.setup: Annie is skeptical that the ID Jeff procured looks like her
jokes.punchline: Jeff's dismissive 'She's a white brunette' reduces Annie's identity to two demographic descriptors, and Annie's retort — invoking Anne Hathaway as a counterexample — is a sharp comeback that accepts Jeff's reductive logic and uses it against him
jokes.explanation: Clean three-line exchange with a good structure. Jeff's reductiveness is funny and in-character, but Annie's Anne Hathaway retort is the real joke — it's both a valid counterargument and a slightly absurd celebrity reference that lands with good timing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: The Red Door? More like The Pretentious Film Festival Door. It's basically Inception, but with worse lighting and more judgmental people.

jokes.text: Annie worries about the stack of IDs Jeff's friend has. Jeff explains: "Sometimes people sell their ID when they're leaving the state and need cash." Britta: "So she's a drifter." Jeff: "A floater." Annie: "An urchin."
jokes.setup: Annie is concerned about the source of the fake ID
jokes.punchline: The three characters riff-escalate through increasingly Victorian synonyms for vagrant — 'drifter,' 'floater,' 'urchin' — each building on the last in a spontaneous group bit
jokes.explanation: Good escalating group bit. 'Urchin' as the final escalation is perfect — it's the most archaic and vaguely Dickensian of the three options, which is a funny tonal choice for describing a college student who sold her ID. The three-part structure is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I don't need help. I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? No, I can totally get up these stairs myself.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Stop looking at me like that. My leg will be fine in a few minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, fine, maybe just... hold the door open. But that's it.

jokes.text: Annie reads her new identity: "Caroline Decker from Corpus Christi, Texas." Annie: "Texas? Do I need an accent?" Britta: "You don't need an accent." Annie immediately: "Howdy, y'all. I'm Caroline Decker." Britta: "Please don't do that."
jokes.setup: Annie is nervous about using a fake ID from Texas and asks if she needs an accent
jokes.punchline: Despite being told she doesn't need an accent, Annie immediately launches into an exaggerated Southern drawl — the joke is that she was going to do it regardless of the answer
jokes.explanation: The joke structure is in the gap between the advice given and Annie's immediate non-compliance — she asked as a formality. Britta's 'Please don't do that' is the punchline button. Establishes a running gag that will pay off throughout the bar scenes.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, people are selling fake IDs? That's illegal! And irresponsible! And... and deeply immoral!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Do you know what happens to people who use fake IDs? They become criminals. Career criminals. Hardened criminals with tattoos and no respect for their mothers.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: And then they can't get into good colleges, so they go to community college, and then they have to associate with people like... well, people I shouldn't judge, but clearly I am judging them right now for their life choices.

jokes.text: "I guarantee." Britta: "That's Cajun."
jokes.setup: Annie is practicing her Texas accent and says 'I guarantee' as a Texas-ism
jokes.punchline: Britta flatly corrects that 'I guarantee' is a Cajun (Louisiana) phrase, not Texan — exposing Annie's lack of regional research
jokes.explanation: Two-word punchline with high comedy value. The specific incorrectness (not just wrong Southern, but specifically Cajun) suggests Britta has enough regional knowledge to notice, which is itself a small character moment. Maximum economy — the joke is entirely in 'That's Cajun.'

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Y'all come back now, ya hear?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's not a Texas accent, that's a generic Southern accent. Texas has its own distinct phonetic patterns.

jokes.text: "Flannahan's Hole is closed." Jeff: "That's not a..." "I mean it's out of business." Jeff: "Well, that's what they get for trying to please everyone."
jokes.setup: Everyone converges on Flannahan's Hole as the compromise bar; they arrive to find it closed
jokes.punchline: Jeff's initial reaction of 'That's not a...' (hearing 'Flannahan's Hole is closed' as a crude innuendo) followed by his pivot to earnest bar-economics commentary ('that's what they get for trying to please everyone') lands two jokes in rapid succession
jokes.explanation: The 'That's not a...' double-take on the bar's name being announced as 'closed' is a cute innuendo catch, and 'that's what they get for trying to please everyone' is a perfectly cynical Jeff observation delivered as genuine folk wisdom. Good two-beat structure.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: She probably uses her ID to get into clubs where they don't card, buys alcohol for parties she wasn't invited to, and tells people she's 'basically a model' when she's just really pretty and has good lighting.

jokes.text: Jeff describes an alternative bar: "It's fun-divey, but not Staph infection-divey. It's either got a gross name or an ironically fancy one, possibly both. Oh, The Ballroom."
jokes.setup: Jeff is suggesting a new bar after Flannahan's Hole is closed
jokes.punchline: His taxonomy of dive bars — the 'fun-divey vs. Staph-infection-divey' spectrum and the 'gross name or ironically fancy name, possibly both' prediction — is delivered as confident insider knowledge and proves immediately correct ('The Ballroom')
jokes.explanation: Jeff's bar taxonomy is genuinely observational — the 'gross name or ironically fancy one, possibly both' formula describes a real phenomenon and is funny precisely because it's true. The immediate confirmation ('The Ballroom' = ironically fancy) is a satisfying payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what every dive bar is called? Either 'The Rusty [Something]' or '[Something] Tavern.' That's it. Those are the only two options. 'The Rusty Nail,' 'The Rusty Bucket,' 'McCarthy's Tavern,' 'Flannery's Tavern.' It's like dive bars are named by a computer program that only has two templates.

jokes.text: "The women are your problem, and the men are going to The Ballroom. And now I guess I am being clever."
jokes.setup: Earlier Jeff said 'That's what they get for trying to please everyone' and added 'and now I'm not being clever' — now he splits the group and says the bar's name
jokes.punchline: Jeff acknowledges that The Ballroom, as a name for a bar, makes his earlier non-clever statement now retroactively clever — a small meta-wink at his own wit
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-aware callback to his own almost-pun is a small but satisfying structural note. It's a bit inside-baseball (you need to have caught the earlier self-deprecation) but rewards attentive viewers. The light meta-touch is very Community.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: The Ballroom? That's where they keep all the balls.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, I see what I did there.

jokes.text: Jeff's speech to Troy about entering 'the final chapter' of life — "Sadly, it's the final chapter, but it's also the longest, and if you play it right, the best." Troy: "So awesome. Maybe later you'll let me drive your car." Jeff: "No way. No."
jokes.setup: Jeff delivers a sincere-seeming mentorship speech about Troy entering adulthood as 'peers, equals'
jokes.punchline: Troy immediately tests the new 'peers, equals' dynamic by asking to drive Jeff's car, and Jeff reflexively shuts it down — the whole egalitarian speech evaporating instantly
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom structure done well: a speech sets up sincere sentiment, then a single line deflates the pretension. 'No way. No.' is perfect — the double refusal, the slight panic in the rhythm, and Jeff's total lack of hesitation reveal that his vision of 'peers, equals' had no actual application. Strong character integration for both — Jeff's self-serving magnanimity and Troy's naïve literalism.

jokes.text: Shirley enters the bar saying she doesn't like it; then the bartender says 'Welcome back, Shirley' and she urgently, repeatedly insists 'You don't know me.'
jokes.setup: Shirley has been dismissive and judgmental about the bar choice all episode, implying she's too good for dive bars
jokes.punchline: The bartender's 'Welcome back' reveals Shirley is a known regular — completely contradicting her squeaky-clean, church-going persona — and her panicked 'You don't know me. Okay? You don't — know me.' is both funny and sad
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural jokes. The entire setup has been Shirley performing sanctimony about bars, and the payoff is devastating in its efficiency — a bartender who knows her name does all the work. Her repeated denial is both the joke and the beginning of genuine character depth. This is the kind of joke that only lands this hard because the show has been building Shirley's self-presentation all episode. Very strong character integration: this is ONLY possible with Shirley. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and arguably above it for structural setup and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Troy's entering a new chapter of his life. You know what that means? He's one chapter closer to the end of the book. And the ending of this book is death.

jokes.text: "These pictures must be of all the regulars. You think someday I could make it up to this wall?" Jeff: "I don't say this often, Troy, but — dream a little smaller."
jokes.setup: Troy looks at the bar's wall of regulars and aspires to be on it
jokes.punchline: Jeff, usually the one to encourage grand ambitions (or at least claim to), tells Troy to dream smaller — implying that aspiring to be a known regular at a bar is a depressingly low life goal
jokes.explanation: 'Dream a little smaller' is a great inversion of the inspirational mentor trope. Jeff usually plays aspirational with Troy, so the reversal — combined with the specific bleakness of what Troy is aspiring to — lands well. The 'I don't say this often' setup heightens the expectation before the deflation. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: Shirley! Long time no see!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh, no, I think you have me confused with someone else.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: No, it's definitely you. You used to come in here every night.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That was... a different time in my life. I'm a changed woman now. A Christian woman.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: Right, right. Can I get you something?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Just a... a virgin daiquiri. Very virgin. Like, aggressively virgin.

jokes.text: Annie in the bar uses her Texas persona, ordering water in a Southern accent. Bartender: "Where's that accent from?" Annie: "Corpus Christi, Texas. 78418."
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to maintain her fake Texas identity at the bar
jokes.punchline: She answers the question of where her accent is from, then voluntarily adds the ZIP code — the kind of over-prepared detail that makes the cover story instantly suspicious
jokes.explanation: The ZIP code is the perfect Annie-specific detail. She prepared too much — over-researched her cover story and can't resist deploying all of it, which is exactly what someone who is not a relaxed improviser would do. Very strong character integration: this joke literally couldn't work for anyone else in the group. 'I should research Corpus Christi' callback pays off here.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You really think I could make it to the wall of regulars?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, Troy, I don't want to lower your expectations, but... actually, no, I do. Yes, lower them. Lower them a lot.

jokes.text: Annie, continuing her Texas persona, describes herself to the bartender: "Not much, I reckon. Just... drifting, floating. Spittin' in the wind. General waywardness."
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to embody the free-spirited persona of Caroline Decker (the ID's owner, described as a 'drifter, floater, urchin')
jokes.punchline: She recycles the exact words her friends used to describe the ID's original owner ('drifting, floating') and adds 'General waywardness' — which sounds like a bureaucratic category rather than a lifestyle description, betraying her planner's brain
jokes.explanation: Smart callback: Annie literally memorized the descriptors her friends used and is now deploying them as lifestyle choices. 'General waywardness' is the tell — it sounds like a checkbox on a form, not a character's self-description. This reveals Annie's compulsive preparation even when trying to be spontaneous, which is the thematic core of her arc this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: Where are you from?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Greendale, Colorado. Zip code 80401. Population 6,247 as of the 2010 census. Elevation 5,427 feet above sea level.

jokes.text: "Annie, you're in the bar. You don't have to be from Texas anymore."
jokes.setup: Annie is still performing the Texas accent and persona at the bar even after successfully getting in
jokes.punchline: Britta points out the obvious — the ID was just to get in, not an ongoing performance requirement — which Annie apparently didn't realize
jokes.explanation: Good beat that shows Annie has gotten so deep into her performance she's lost sight of the purpose. Britta's matter-of-fact correction is funny in its clarity. Sets up Annie's deeper arc about identity.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: What's Caroline doing in town?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh, she's just... living her best life. Moving from place to place, no strings attached, following her heart wherever it takes her. It's so romantic when you think about it.

jokes.text: "I don't know how it works. I'm not a bar-fly, Britta." [sees Asteroids machine] "They have 'Asteroids.' Slide out."
jokes.setup: Britta tells Annie she can drop the Texas persona; Annie protests she doesn't know bar etiquette
jokes.punchline: The moment Annie spots an Asteroids machine, she drops all anxiety and immediately says 'Slide out' — reverting to her actual self (a nerdy game-player) the second something familiar appears
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Annie's anxiety about bar culture evaporates the second she sees something from her comfort zone. The pacing ('Slide out' — just two words, completely changing energy) is excellent. Thematically relevant to her arc about identity.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay Troy, your first legal drink. This is a big moment. You want something smooth, approachable.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm thinking maybe a beer?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Classic choice. Good instinct.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Or you could go with whiskey. Shows confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Whiskey? Kid, whiskey is a journey. It's about understanding the transience of pleasure and the inevitability of regret.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That's beautiful, Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm not done. Every sip is a meditation on mortality. The burn in your throat? That's your soul waking up to the fact that we're all just temporary vessels in an indifferent universe.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'll have a Sprite.

jokes.text: Jeff and Troy debate Troy's first legal drink. Troy: "I like beer." Jeff: "Don't order beer. You've had beer." Troy: "What should I get?" Jeff: "Follow your heart." Troy: "My Uncle Carl played a big role in my life... His favourite drink was a seven and seven." Jeff and Britta simultaneously: "Don't order that. That's an awful drink. A high school drink for girls."
jokes.setup: Troy is choosing his first legal drink and touches on a sincere emotional memory of his late Uncle Carl
jokes.punchline: The moment Troy invokes his uncle's legacy drink, Jeff and Britta BOTH immediately and harshly dismiss it — the emotional sincerity of the memory crashing against the snobbery of the response ('a high school drink for girls')
jokes.explanation: The joke works through tonal collision: Troy's earnest emotional tribute is met with instant, synchronized snobbery. The fact that Jeff AND Britta — who never agree on bars — are united in their contempt for the seven and seven is the best part. The escalation from 'Don't order that' to 'a high school drink for girls' is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I want seven and seven to honor my dead uncle.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Your uncle was a drink?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: He loved seven and sevens!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Troy, your uncle was an alcoholic who drank himself to death. You're not honoring him, you're just making excuses to get drunk.

jokes.text: Annie, playing Asteroids and in full Texas mode, is approached by a man at the machine. She references The Last Starfighter. He responds with Farscape knowledge. This leads to Abed appearing: "You're a fan of the sci-fi original series Farscape."
jokes.setup: Annie is playing Asteroids; a man approaches with a sci-fi Asteroids joke ('the Rylans are gonna recruit you to fight the Ko-Dan Empire' — Last Starfighter reference)
jokes.punchline: He and Annie bond over Farscape knowledge; Abed materializes and identifies the man as 'a fan of the sci-fi original series Farscape' — as if announcing the category of person he's found rather than making conversation
jokes.explanation: Abed's identification of the man as a Farscape fan is perfect — he's categorizing a human specimen rather than socializing. 'You're a fan of the sci-fi original series Farscape' is stated as a clinical conclusion, not an opener. This is very specifically Abed behavior. The whole sequence also shows Annie being herself (the nerd) despite trying to be Caroline Decker, which is thematically resonant.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm getting recruited by an intergalactic arcade game company to fight aliens in space.

dialogue.speaker: Robert
dialogue.line: That's... just the plot of The Last Starfighter.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Robert (the bar patron): "Can I buy you a drink?" — said to Abed, not Annie
jokes.setup: Robert has been talking to Annie/Abed about Farscape; we expect him to be hitting on Annie
jokes.punchline: He asks Abed for a drink — the camera lingering on the moment before Abed processes it
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — the whole exchange has been coded as the man flirting with Annie while Abed tags along, so the pivot to Abed is a clean subversion. Sets up the extended sequence that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Robert
dialogue.line: You know a lot about sci-fi.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, I've seen most of the classics.

dialogue.speaker: Robert
dialogue.line: Want to get together and watch some movies sometime?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Sure, that sounds cool.

jokes.text: Pierce tries to get into the bar; bouncer asks for ID. Pierce: "Very funny, punk. Get out of my way!" Pierce: "I don't know how people like you even get jobs."
jokes.setup: Pierce (elderly, in a wheelchair) is being carded at the bar
jokes.punchline: Pierce treats being ID'd as an obviously absurd insult ('Very funny, punk') and then immediately insults the bouncer's employment — his indignation escalating inversely to any reasonable response
jokes.explanation: Pierce's obliviousness works here — a visibly elderly man in a wheelchair treating being carded as a personal affront is a good character beat. The move to 'I don't know how people like you even get jobs' is a bit of casual elitist contempt that feels very Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: People think I'm really smart and sophisticated.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I mean, I had to tell them I was... ubiquitous.

jokes.text: Pierce: "Oh, you'd like that, wouldn't you? A little turning of the tables? Hah." Bouncer: "The turning of what tables?" Pierce: "I don't know, leave me alone!"
jokes.setup: Someone (likely Troy or Jeff) offers to help Pierce with the ID/entry situation
jokes.punchline: Pierce imagines this as 'a turning of the tables' — some elaborate power dynamic reversal — but when asked to explain, he has nothing and retreats to 'leave me alone'
jokes.explanation: Pierce's conspiratorial paranoia producing a phrase ('turning of the tables') that he can't actually define is a strong character moment. The bouncer's genuinely confused 'The turning of what tables?' deflates the pomposity perfectly, and Pierce's retreat to 'leave me alone' is a satisfying collapse. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It means unpredictable. Like the weather, or my emotions.

jokes.text: "So I punched her. Right in the face." Annie: "Your probation officer?" Britta: "Didn't you get in trouble?" "Hell yes I got in trouble! Wasn't the first time, won't be the last. I'm not exactly known for my sound judgement."
jokes.setup: Britta is sharing a story, apparently about an altercation
jokes.punchline: The reveal that she punched her probation officer — and her completely unbothered, self-aware acknowledgment ('I'm not exactly known for my sound judgement') — recontextualizes Britta as someone with a genuinely wild past
jokes.explanation: Good character-deepening moment played as a joke. Britta punching her probation officer is a genuinely surprising revelation given how we've seen her perform righteousness all episode. 'I'm not exactly known for my sound judgement' delivered with casual self-awareness is both funny and characterologically rich.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What are you ordering, a 'Britta-ny Spears'?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Actually, it's called a 'Britta-ccino.' Get it? Because my name is Britta and it's a cappuccino?

jokes.text: Annie, still in Caroline Decker mode, tells Britta: "Back in Corpus Christi, they call me Capricious Caroline." Bartender: "What's 'capricious' mean?" Annie: "It probably means I'm too busy living life to be learning $5 words."
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to embody the free-spirited Caroline Decker persona and uses the word 'capricious'
jokes.punchline: When asked what 'capricious' means, Annie-as-Caroline says she's 'too busy living life to learn $5 words' — which inadvertently reveals that Annie absolutely knows what capricious means (she chose the word deliberately) while performing ignorance
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. The irony operates on two levels: Annie knows what capricious means (she's Annie), and her attempt to cover this by claiming she's too spontaneous to learn vocabulary reveals the opposite — a meticulous planner who chose 'capricious' specifically. The '$5 words' construction is very funny coming from someone who could use 'capricious' correctly in a sentence. Very strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'll have a... caramel macchiato-tini.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's not a real drink.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Exactly. Neither is half the stuff people order.

jokes.text: Jeff lectures Troy on Scotch: "With an aged Scotch, never use ice. Never use ice." Troy: "Why?" Jeff: "Destroys it. At most, two drops of spring water. Activates the flavour."
jokes.setup: Jeff is mentoring Troy on how to drink properly
jokes.punchline: Jeff's pedantic Scotch instructions are delivered as absolute law — the 'two drops of spring water' rule delivered with the same gravity as a life principle. This is funny because it's real (Scotch drinkers do say this) but also because Jeff is performing expertise
jokes.explanation: Functional observational humor about drink snobbery. Gets the job done but isn't special — this joke could work in many shows. Its main value is in setting up Shirley's response.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I need to go powder my nose.

jokes.text: Shirley: "Do they have the rules to high-maintenance poser drinking on the wall at L Street? Do they?" Jeff: "'Poser drinking'? Hey, Ms. Vodka-Neat-Four-Olives. What's that called? The 'Too Cool To Care'-tini?"
jokes.setup: Jeff is being a Scotch snob; Shirley calls him out for 'poser drinking'
jokes.punchline: Jeff immediately fires back at Shirley's earlier drink order ('Vodka neat, four olives'), naming it the 'Too Cool To Care'-tini — exposing that Shirley's own drink order was also an affectation
jokes.explanation: 'Too Cool To Care'-tini is a great invention — the name perfectly skewers a certain type of studied nonchalance. Jeff catching Shirley's hypocrisy is both funny and fair. Good callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You're like a hurricane, Annie.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: A hurricane? But you're not even wet, and there's no wind in here.

jokes.text: Troy: "I can't wait to understand these arguments."
jokes.setup: Jeff and Shirley are arguing about drink snobbery in a way Troy can't yet parse
jokes.punchline: Troy's patient, sincere 'I can't wait to understand these arguments' treats the snobbery debate as a form of adult wisdom he aspires to rather than meaningless bickering
jokes.explanation: Perfect Troy line. The joke is in what it doesn't say — most people watching would dismiss the Jeff/Shirley argument as pointless posturing, but Troy is genuinely excited to one day be knowledgeable enough to participate. His earnestness transforms the moment and delivers a sharp implicit commentary on the arbitrariness of adult status markers. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Robert
dialogue.line: Did it hurt? When you fell through a wormhole?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Wormholes don't work that way. They're theoretical constructs that would require exotic matter with negative energy density to stabilize. Also, I didn't fall through anything. I'm standing right here.

jokes.text: Annie-as-Caroline introduces herself to the bartender: "Y'all are so nice in this town. I'm Caroline. From Corpus Christi. I grew up on a trout farm. Deedily doo."
jokes.setup: Annie continues to perform her Caroline Decker persona
jokes.punchline: 'Deedily doo' as a capper — Annie's invention of Southern folksy filler language reaches its logical breaking point with a completely invented phrase
jokes.explanation: 'Deedily doo' is the moment Annie's performance completely leaves the rails. The escalation from somewhat-plausible Southern affectations to made-up filler sounds is well-paced. Good running gag payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I don't plan things. I'm like a beautiful Southern belle who just lets life happen to her, like a magnolia blossom in the wind.

jokes.text: Robert tells Abed: "Abed, I actually did pick up on [you hitting on me] after a while." Abed: "And?" Robert: "I really, really like talking about Farscape."
jokes.setup: Robert has revealed he was hitting on Abed; Abed says he knew but kept talking anyway
jokes.punchline: Robert's explanation — he tolerated (or maybe enjoyed?) the implied flirtation because Farscape conversation was more important — is a perfect, economical encapsulation of nerd prioritization
jokes.explanation: Robert's 'I really, really like talking about Farscape' as the explanation for enduring an unwanted come-on is both funny and genuinely sweet. The 'really, really' is perfect emphasis. The joke also says something true: for certain people, shared passion transcends awkward social dynamics. Gets a rewatch bonus for the warmth beneath the comedy. Near the 8.0 anchor in quality.

jokes.text: Robert and Abed continue the Farscape debate: "Stargate is better." [long pause implied]
jokes.setup: Robert and Abed have been deeply bonding over Farscape
jokes.punchline: Robert casually drops 'Stargate is better' as a conversation-ender — the sci-fi equivalent of a grenade — after their entire connection was built on Farscape appreciation
jokes.explanation: The abrupt pivot from connection to sci-fi heresy in three words is very funny. The implication that this single statement ends the Farscape conversation is a good button to the entire subplot. Maximum economy — the joke exists entirely in those three words at that moment.

dialogue.speaker: Robert
dialogue.line: Why didn't you pick up on her hitting on you?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: She was talking about how the latest Star Trek film ignored established canon. I had to correct her on the Kelvin Timeline. That takes priority.

jokes.text: Robert: 'You know, speaking of wormholes, what do you say we use one to teleport this conversation some place a little more private?' Abed: 'That doesn't make any sense. Wormholes and teleportation are two different things. That's what I've been talking about this whole time.'
jokes.setup: Robert has been using sci-fi conversation as a lead-up to a pick-up line
jokes.punchline: Abed rejects the metaphor on scientific grounds — not because he understands it's a come-on, but because the sci-fi terminology is wrong. He's oblivious to the subtext and focused only on accuracy.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Abed joke — he doesn't reject the advance because he's straight or uninterested; he rejects the METAPHOR because it's scientifically incorrect. The scene then continues where Abed IS aware of the come-on but kept talking because he likes Farscape more. The joke rewards Abed's specific brand of social disconnection: not autism played for pity, but a genuinely different value system (accuracy over social convention).

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Lord, I'm praying for the souls in these photographs.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Shirley, that photo of you was found in the men's bathroom at the bus station.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: What?!

jokes.text: "It's a funny picture because you act so perfect all the time. And because you look like a zombie."
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining why Shirley's photo is funny
jokes.punchline: He gives two separate reasons — one character-based ('you act so perfect all the time') and one purely visual ('you look like a zombie') — the second one landing as an afterthought that's funnier for its casualness
jokes.explanation: The 'zombie' addition works as an escalation — the first reason is thematic, the second is visual and blunt. Jeff's matter-of-fact delivery of 'you look like a zombie' as a secondary observation is funnier than if it were the main point.

jokes.text: "But it's not funny when you're sad. We're on your team. Relax, sit down." Shirley: "It's my birthday." Everyone: "It's Troy's birthday." Shirley: "Give it to me."
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to comfort Shirley after the photo embarrassment
jokes.punchline: In the middle of this ostensibly sincere moment of group support, Shirley tries to claim it's her birthday to redirect attention — and everyone immediately corrects that it's Troy's birthday, not hers
jokes.explanation: Decent beat — Shirley's desperate claim of birthday status to get the photo back is funny in its transparent manipulation. The group's simultaneous correction is a good reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: You're welcome, Pierce. I'm always happy to help.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Even though you're a terrible person and nobody likes you.

jokes.text: Shirley storms out saying 'I will see you all on Monday' — everyone responds with exaggerated despair ('Sheeeeesh,' 'Mm-hm,' 'Boo Town').
jokes.setup: Shirley is leaving in a huff after the photo embarrassment
jokes.punchline: 'Boo Town' as Abed's response — an oddly precise piece of slang that nonetheless perfectly captures the mood
jokes.explanation: 'Boo Town' is a good Abed-ism — formal enough to sound like he's naming a place or concept, casual enough to feel like slang. The combination of responses (the elongated 'Sheeeesh,' the neutral 'Mm-hm,' and 'Boo Town') creates a funny tonal spread.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You mean L Street? The one with the red door?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yes, that's what I've been saying.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's the same place! We've been arguing about the same place this whole time!

jokes.text: Pierce, in his wheelchair, claims he 'can't get out of the way' because 'the chair broke' — but then asks Shirley 'pretty please' to help him. Shirley: "You're welcome, jackass."
jokes.setup: Pierce stops Shirley from leaving, ostensibly to say something meaningful
jokes.punchline: His reason for stopping her is that his wheelchair is stuck and he needs her to move him — his apparent moment of connection was actually a request for help he was too proud to ask for directly. Shirley's 'You're welcome, jackass' closes it perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff to the 'I'm not a disabled' joke. Pierce spent the whole episode refusing help for his chair, and now he needs it and has to ask. The 'pretty please' is a great character beat — he's too proud for a simple request so it comes out weirdly formal. Shirley's 'You're welcome, jackass' is a great button that's warm and cutting simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You guys have been arguing about Paddy's the whole time?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Paddy's. That's the bar. You've both been describing Paddy's.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, I was talking about—

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Paddy's. It's Paddy's.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Could you -- pl-please help me? Pretty please?' Shirley: 'You're welcome, jackass.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has just witnessed Shirley's emotional moment and her storming out; he calls after her, apparently moved — but it turns out his chair is stuck and he actually needs her help
jokes.punchline: Pierce's apparent emotional moment was just him being trapped; his 'pretty please' is humiliating; and Shirley's 'You're welcome, jackass' — thanking him before he's thanked her — delivers warmth and contempt simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Good subverted-sentimentality joke — Pierce's apparent emotional connection was physical necessity, which is funnier because we briefly hoped for more. 'You're welcome, jackass' is a perfect Shirley line — she helps him while maintaining her opinion of him. Nice beat in what could've been a purely sentimental moment.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We're not going to a bar. We're going to a hospital. Because that's where you go when you get stabbed. Which is what's going to happen at a bar.

jokes.text: Troy at midnight: "It's my birthday and technically I'm not allowed to drink it for another 45 seconds... well, actually it'll be 30 seconds by the time I'm done saying this, but — can I have a seven and seven?" Bartender: "It's on the house."
jokes.setup: Troy is ordering his first legal drink at midnight; Jeff and Britta previously told him NOT to order a seven and seven
jokes.punchline: Troy orders the seven and seven anyway — the drink he was told was 'awful' and 'a high school drink for girls' — in memory of Uncle Carl, completing his emotional arc for the evening
jokes.explanation: This is both a funny joke (the callback to the dismissed drink) and genuinely earned emotionally. Troy's specificity about the seconds ('45... well actually 30 by the time I finish saying this') is a perfect character beat — it's Troy being Troy even in a meaningful moment. His quiet insistence on the seven and seven despite being told not to is a small act of self-determination that lands as both funny and touching. The bartender's 'On the house' is a warm close to the moment. This is the episode's best callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know, alcohol is like a truth serum, except it also makes you forget the truth you just told.

jokes.text: Annie-as-Caroline is talking to two men at the bar. We hear fragments: "A radio playing would be totally horrible... I'd rather have my eyes gouged out..."
jokes.setup: Annie is continuing her Caroline Decker persona at the bar, apparently bonding with people
jokes.punchline: Caroline Decker, as a free-spirited drifter, apparently has very strong negative opinions about something mundane enough to be funny — the fragments suggest she's being gratuitously extreme about something trivial
jokes.explanation: Difficult to fully score since we only get fragments, but the gag seems to be Annie performing extreme opinions as a character quirk. Weaker than other Annie-as-Caroline jokes because it's not specific enough to fully land.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie, you have an almost obsessive need for validation and approval from authority figures, which stems from your childhood perfectionism and fear of failure.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's... surprisingly accurate.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I know. I read it off the back of a psychology book I found in the library.

jokes.text: Jeff, cradling drunk Troy like a baby: "My big boy. Big, big boy. You're my big boy."
jokes.setup: Jeff spent the whole episode talking about Troy becoming a man and their new 'peer' relationship
jokes.punchline: With Troy now drunk and helpless, Jeff is literally coddling him like an infant, saying 'My big boy' — the peak irony of the episode's 'Troy becomes a man' theme
jokes.explanation: Perfect thematic reversal of the 'peers, equals' speech. The image of Jeff cradling a drunk Troy while calling him 'my big boy' is the visual embodiment of the episode's argument that becoming an adult isn't a single moment. The repetition ('Big, big boy') is funnier than a single iteration — it has a lullaby rhythm. Good rewatch value as it crystallizes the episode's theme in a funny image.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie's got like a... a binder system. Not just one binder. Multiple binders. Color-coded. With tabs. And she laminated the tabs. Who laminates tabs? Annie does. She also has a label maker. A personal label maker. Not borrowed. It's hers. She named it.

jokes.text: "Crash it, Troy." Abed: "Go to sleep, Abed." "Crash his car, Troy."
jokes.setup: Jeff lets Troy drive his car; Britta is drunk in the backseat
jokes.punchline: Drunk Britta keeps telling Troy to crash Jeff's car; Jeff tells her to go to sleep; she continues anyway — the loop is funny in its persistence and in what it reveals about Britta's feelings toward Jeff
jokes.explanation: Good drunk-Britta character beat. Her continued insistence after being told to go to sleep is funny, and 'Crash his car' as a phrase is funnier each time it's repeated. The implied antagonism toward Jeff from Britta reads as a whole relationship dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, I've been standing here the whole time. You guys are making out and I'm just... not being acknowledged.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's like I'm invisible. Which, granted, is what I wanted in high school, but now it's just depressing.

jokes.text: Abed: "This seems like a really dark chapter in our group story." Jeff: "Go to sleep, Abed." Abed: "Cool."
jokes.setup: Everyone is drunk and Troy is driving Jeff's car
jokes.punchline: Abed narrates the moment as a 'dark chapter in our group story' — framing lived experience as a narrative — then accepts the instruction to stop with a simple 'Cool'
jokes.explanation: Very strong Abed joke. 'Dark chapter in our group story' is a perfect Abed-ism — he experiences life as narrative and this is an extremely honest version of that tendency, delivered at an inappropriate moment (while drunk in a moving car). The 'Cool' acceptance is a perfect button: he has no emotional investment in whether he's told to stop, he was just narrating. High character integration — this only works as Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: I need help with something urgent!

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: What's wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: I... I really need to use the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: Oh. Um. The bathroom is...

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: I know where it is! I just can't... get there by myself right now.

jokes.text: Jeff and Britta argue about L Street vs. the Red Door as Troy drives; Troy points at a sign: "Hey, that's the place we should've gone tonight." Jeff: "Yeah, L Street, exactly." Britta: "That's the Red Door, stupid." "Do you see a sign that says L Street?" "L Street is too cool to have a sign. It's called L Street after the street it's on."
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta have argued all episode about L Street vs. the Red Door
jokes.punchline: Jeff claims L Street is too cool to have a sign; Britta reveals the Red Door IS on L Street — setting up the revelation
jokes.explanation: Setup for the episode's best structural payoff. 'L Street is too cool to have a sign' is a great piece of Jeff logic — he would absolutely believe that — and it sets up the revelation perfectly. Good structure score for how well this sequence has been planted.

jokes.text: "The Red Door is on L Street. L Street has a red..." [pause] "Hey — it's the same bar?!"
jokes.setup: Britta has told Jeff the Red Door is on L Street; Jeff is processing this in real time
jokes.punchline: Jeff's dawning realization — delivered mid-sentence as the logic assembles itself — that he and Britta have been arguing about the same bar all night is the episode's funniest structural payoff
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke in terms of structural craft. The entire Jeff/Britta bar argument — which has driven their subplot for the whole episode — is revealed to be completely meaningless because they've been talking about the same place. The mid-sentence revelation ('L Street has a red...') as Jeff's voice trails off and then returns with the full force of the realization is perfect comedy construction. It also retroactively makes every exchange funnier on rewatch. This is what Community does better than most shows — building structural comedy over an entire episode. Very close to the 9.5 anchor in terms of structural craft, though not quite at that cultural-touchstone level of quotability.

jokes.text: "You two have been saying one bar's lame and the other is awesome all night, and it's the same... bar?!" Jeff: "Well, he probably goes there on Friday nights, which is lame." Britta: "You wish..."
jokes.setup: Troy has just witnessed the revelation that the two bars are the same
jokes.punchline: Jeff and Britta IMMEDIATELY begin re-litigating their argument using the new information ('Friday nights are lame') rather than accepting they were both wrong
jokes.explanation: The immediate pivot from revelation to re-argument is the episode's best character moment. Neither Jeff nor Britta pauses to feel embarrassed — they instantly reconfigure their snobbery around the new information. This is excellent character integration: their need to be right overrides everything. The speed of the comeback is what makes it land so hard. 'You wish...' from Britta is a perfect button.

jokes.text: "Just stop. I just spent the last two years thinking that you guys knew more than me about life, and I just found out that you guys are just as dumb as me. Duh-doy."
jokes.setup: Troy has watched Jeff and Britta immediately begin re-arguing despite having been exposed as idiots
jokes.punchline: 'Duh-doy' — Troy's invented word for a self-evident truth — delivered as the punchline to an entire episode's worth of setup about Troy learning adult wisdom
jokes.explanation: The best joke of the episode and potentially a contender for one of the series' best Troy moments. The speech is both the thematic core of the episode AND the punchline — Troy's realization that adults are just as confused as he is, delivered with the perfect anti-climactic 'duh-doy.' What elevates this beyond a standard revelation speech is 'duh-doy' — a word that Troy apparently invented that means something everyone already knew but shouldn't have needed to say. The fact that Jeff and Britta then BOTH say 'duh-doy' (instead of being chastened) makes it even funnier. This is approaching the 9.5 anchor in terms of character integration and earned delivery — it's the culmination of the whole episode's comedic argument.

jokes.text: Jeff: "Duh-doy." Britta: "Yeah. Duh-doy." Troy: "Got it. Duh-doy."
jokes.setup: Troy has just said 'duh-doy' as a concluding put-down
jokes.punchline: Jeff and Britta both immediately adopt 'duh-doy' — the word they've just been told they deserve — confirming they have no self-awareness, and Troy's 'Got it. Duh-doy.' closes the loop
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to the duh-doy sequence. Jeff and Britta adopting the word without irony is the funniest possible response — they've been told they're dumb and they accept the new vocabulary as proof of cool. Troy's 'Got it. Duh-doy.' closes the circle. The three-beat repetition builds to something bigger than any individual line.

jokes.text: "You can take me home first. I only live a few blocks from here." Troy: "You do?" Annie: "Yeah." Long pause. Troy: "Annie, this is a really terrible neighbourhood."
jokes.setup: Annie asks to be dropped off first at her apartment
jokes.punchline: The pause before Troy responds, then his simple observation that it's a terrible neighborhood — played as genuine concern rather than judgment — lands as both funny and sad
jokes.explanation: The awkward silence beat before Troy responds is key — everyone is processing that Annie lives alone in a bad neighborhood, and the silence does comedic and emotional work simultaneously. Troy's sincere concern ('a really terrible neighbourhood') is a character moment for him, and the 'Yeah.' that follows is quietly devastating.

jokes.text: "Alcohol makes people sad. It's like the Lifetime movies of beverages."
jokes.setup: Troy and Britta have just watched a night of people's drinking-related misadventures
jokes.punchline: Troy's summary of alcohol as 'the Lifetime movies of beverages' — both implying he watches Lifetime movies and finding the perfect cultural analogy for a substance that promises fun and delivers sadness
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the episode. 'The Lifetime movies of beverages' is an extraordinary construction — it works on multiple levels: Lifetime movies promise melodrama and deliver exactly what they promise (suffering), which is what alcohol does. It also implies Troy is familiar with Lifetime movies, which is a small additional character note. The economy is near-perfect — the entire theme of the episode (adults behaving badly in bars) compressed into eight words. Very quotable, memorable, and original. Comparable to or slightly above the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Annie tells Britta: "I pretended to be a different person tonight." Britta: "Abed does that, like three times a week."
jokes.setup: Annie is having a sincere moment about identity and her Caroline Decker performance
jokes.punchline: Britta deflects the earnestness by pointing out that Abed performs characters constantly — which is completely true — undercutting Annie's self-analysis without being cruel
jokes.explanation: Good deflation joke that is also a true observation about Abed. 'Three times a week' is a funny specific quantity — not 'all the time' but enough to be notable. Britta's point inadvertently raises the question of whether Abed's character-performance is a coping mechanism, which the show explores elsewhere.

jokes.text: Troy's speech about knowing Annie: "You like puzzles, and... little monsters on your pencil and some guy named Mark Ruffalo. You're a fierce competitor and a sore loser. And... you expect everybody to be better than who they are, and you expect yourself to be better than everyone."
jokes.setup: Annie says they went to school together for four years and he didn't know her
jokes.punchline: Troy proves he does know her with a list of observations — 'little monsters on your pencil' is the funny specific detail amid the more sincere character observations, and 'you expect yourself to be better than everyone' is both a compliment and a slight
jokes.explanation: 'Little monsters on your pencil' is a perfectly chosen detail — specific enough to be funny and true (it's very Annie), placed among more serious character notes so it lands as a tonal contrast. The final line ('expect yourself to be better than everyone') is both a compliment and a mic-drop that shows Troy is more observant than he's given credit for.

jokes.text: Jeff and a woman almost kiss and both pull back: "What are we doing?" "Yeah, what are we doing?" "This is a bad idea, right?" "Yeah."
jokes.setup: Jeff followed Shirley out after she stormed off; they have a moment of genuine connection
jokes.punchline: Both Jeff and Shirley realize they were about to kiss — the mutual, mirrored 'what are we doing' is both the awkward comedy and the actual question
jokes.explanation: More cringe-discomfort than outright joke, but the near-kiss is a comedic beat in context. The rewatch bonus is for how unexpected this pairing is — it rewards knowing Shirley's character. Not a strong joke on its own but serves the episode structure.

jokes.text: "I flew off the handle earlier. I apologize." [pause] "They were making out." Abed: "Abed!" "Why the hell would you say that?" Abed: "Why do it in front of me? I'm not a coat rack."
jokes.setup: Jeff is making a dignified apology to Shirley after their almost-kiss; Abed is apparently present and has witnessed everything
jokes.punchline: Abed immediately announces that they were making out — both a tattletale move and a clinical observation — and when called out, defends himself with 'I'm not a coat rack' (meaning he can't be expected to be ignored just because they want privacy)
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. 'I'm not a coat rack' is a perfect Abed line — it's simultaneously a complaint about being treated as furniture, a logical defense of his right to narrate what he sees, and a bizarrely specific analogy that only Abed would reach for. The sequence has three distinct funny beats: the announcement, the outrage, and the defense. Very high character integration — only Abed would (a) announce this, (b) feel the need to justify it, and (c) compare himself to a coat rack. This is comparable to the 8.0 anchor and arguably above it.

jokes.text: "They were making out." / "Abed!" / "Why the hell would you say that?" / "Why do it in front of me? I'm not a coat rack."
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie have just had a brief romantic moment (implied) in the car; Abed was present
jokes.punchline: Abed announces what happened with documentary precision ('They were making out'), then when challenged, protests that he was an unwilling witness — 'I'm not a coat rack' — implying he was simply part of the furniture during their moment
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Abed moments. 'They were making out' is funny in its clinical precision. But 'I'm not a coat rack' is exceptional — Abed's protest is that his PRESENCE was ignored, not that the act was inappropriate. He resents being treated as furniture, not as a voyeur. The logic is completely Abed. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: "Abed, no one likes a tattletale."
jokes.setup: Abed has just announced to the group that Jeff and Shirley were making out
jokes.punchline: Jeff responds to the most embarrassing possible revelation with the least proportionate rebuke available — 'no one likes a tattletale' — a thing you say to children, not to a witness of adult impropriety
jokes.explanation: Jeff's resort to a playground-level admonishment in response to a genuinely mortifying revelation is a good character beat — he's trying to diminish the incident by using childish framing. The incongruity between the seriousness of the event and the mildness of the response is the joke.

jokes.text: "Happy birthday, Troy." Troy: "Thanks." "You're a man now."
jokes.setup: The episode's theme has been 'Troy becoming a man' at 21; Jeff has just been caught in a near-kiss with Shirley
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers 'you're a man now' with absolutely zero self-awareness given what just happened — the episode's theme of adult wisdom being exposed as false is crystallized in this earnest line delivered by someone who just behaved like a teenager
jokes.explanation: Perfect thematic button to the episode. 'You're a man now' delivered by Jeff — who has just been revealed as making out with Shirley behind a dumpster or similar — has enormous ironic weight. It completes the 'adults are just as dumb as teenagers' argument that Troy articulated with 'duh-doy' but delivers it through pure dramatic irony. Strong structure as a callback to multiple earlier moments.

jokes.text: Pierce struggling to get into something (a jacket? doorway?): "I don't think this is gonna be big enough." "Just try it, we're so close." "Breathe in." "Arms." "There we go."
jokes.setup: Post-bar, Pierce is apparently trying to get back into something — given his wheelchair and broken legs, some normal task is now absurdly difficult
jokes.punchline: The dialogue sounds vaguely suggestive ('big enough,' 'breathe in,' 'arms,' 'there we go') but is apparently about something mundane — the comedy is in the incongruity of the effort required
jokes.explanation: Hard to fully assess from transcript alone — this is primarily a visual gag. The dialogue suggests physical comedy with Pierce's broken-leg situation but without seeing the actual visual, the transcript-only version is weaker. Probably funnier on screen than it reads.

jokes.text: "One hundred and fifty-seven." "We did it!" ... "That you?" "Yeah." "Little help?" "Hurry. I think it's a girl." "Left side or right side?" "Left side." "Tell me when I'm close."
jokes.setup: Post-bar ending sequence — unclear context, but dialogue suggests something is being physically navigated
jokes.punchline: The numbers, the triumphant 'We did it!', 'I think it's a girl,' and 'Tell me when I'm close' all suggest something either suggestive or absurd — the comedy is in the ambiguity and apparent absurdity of whatever is happening
jokes.explanation: This is clearly a visual gag that requires seeing the screen — the transcript only gives us the audio track of something that is primarily physical comedy. 'I think it's a girl' and 'tell me when I'm close' suggest the final gag involves some amusing physical situation. Gets a rewatch bonus because visual payoffs in Community's tag scenes often work better in context. Scoring conservatively given incomplete information.

jokes.text: Post-credits: The group tries to fit something large (implied to be the TV or a couch) through Annie's apartment door — counting to 157 attempts, then triumphantly celebrating
jokes.setup: Post-credits tag: characters are trying to maneuver something through a door
jokes.punchline: They've apparently failed 156 times ('One hundred and fifty-seven. We did it!') and celebrate an absurd persistence in a mundane task with genuine triumph
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist tag — 157 attempts at something is a funny specific number. The implication that the group kept trying for an absurd duration to help Annie is both funny and character-consistent. Probably a visual comedy bit that lands better in performance.

tmdb_overview: Troy's friends help him celebrate his 21st birthday.
insight: Bar crawl episode leans hard on character dynamics over setup-punchline structure.
